title: Ambition, examined

lines: THE RIGHT HAND AND THE LEFT.
cards: Two brothers walk up to their teacher on the road and ask for a favor before they'll say what it is. In Mark's Gospel they are James and John, fishermen who once left their nets to follow Jesus.

The request is blunt: when you come into your glory, let one of us sit at your right hand, and the other at your left. The other ten hear about it, and Mark says they are much displeased. Mark doesn't say why.
Some readers suspect the ten wanted the same seats. Today: ambition.

teach.b: First, what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't tell them to stop wanting to be great. He calls them to him and turns the ladder upside down.
In the King James Bible: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." Ambition isn't erased. It's handed a job.
Second, a voice that climbed all the way up. Ecclesiastes speaks as a king in Jerusalem who built houses, planted vineyards, and gathered silver and gold.

Then he looks at all of it: "all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." He reached what he aimed at, and it couldn't tell him what it was for. Third, a teaching from India.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the work itself, never to its fruits; the fruits shouldn't be his motive, and he shouldn't cling to doing nothing either.
Some readers hear a way to strive with everything while loosening the grip on the prize. Fourth, the question all three leave on the table.
Ambition can serve, or it can consume, and the difference may lie less in how much someone wants than in what the wanting is for.

A promotion that lets someone protect a team is one thing; the same promotion as a scoreboard is another. This week asked about shaping a job, unpaid work, worth without work, stopping, money and sharing.
Ambition asks the question under all of them.

how: Christians read Mark 10:43–44 as a teaching that greatness means serving others, and Hindus who study the Bhagavad Gita read 2.47 as guidance on working fully without clinging to the results.

o: a sin the Gospels tell everyone to give up
plain greed for money, and nothing more
the wish to rise, which Jesus points toward serving

games.q: what's inside ambition — tap the pairs.
p: asked for the seats beside him

s: Jesus tells James and John to stop wanting to be great
he redirects the wish: whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.
the king in Ecclesiastes got what he worked for
houses, vineyards, silver and gold, and still he called it vanity and vexation of spirit.
in the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to stop acting so he won't want results
his right is to the work, not its fruits, and he shouldn't cling to doing nothing either.

games.q: you're one of the other ten disciples, and you've just heard James and John asked for the best seats. what does Mark say the ten did?
o: were much displeased with James and John.
games.why: the ten were much displeased. then Jesus calls them all together and turns greatness into service.

practice: Bring one ambition to mind, large or small: a job, a number, a finished project, a name on a door.
Ask it plainly, what are you for, and ask the same of each answer until the answers stop changing; safety, love, someone you provide for, wanting to be seen: any of these can be honest.
If you pray, hold that last answer in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Ambition. The wish to rise. In Mark's Gospel Jesus doesn't forbid it; he points it toward serving. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 2.47: your right is to the work alone.

carryVoice: Your line: what is it for. The wish can stay; it just needs a job. Day nine hundred seventeen, done.
